en: I bow to the lotus feet of the gurus, who have revealed the realization of the bliss of one's own self; for people, those feet act like a physician’s charm to pacify the delusion that is the halāhala poison of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
The one hundred and twenty-five thousand modes of absorption (laya) taught by Sadāśiva exist in the world;
yet we consider the single samādhi of contemplation upon the primordial sound (nāda) to be the most venerable among all forms of absorption. ||2||

When all the channels have been purified by means of the inhalations, retentions, and exhalations of the breath, the internal sound known as the "Unstruck" (anāhata) shall always resound within in many ways. || 3 ||
Obeisance to you, Nādānusandhāna; I know you to be the means for attaining the state of ultimate reality.
By your grace, my mind dissolves together with the vital breath into the station of Viṣṇu. 4.
They speak of Jālandhara, Uḍḍiyāna, and Mūla-bandha as being located in the throat, the abdomen, and the root of the anus;
when these three bandhas are thoroughly mastered, from where can there be bondage by the terrible noose of Time? 5.
When the serpent-maiden has been awakened by the Oḍyāna, Jālandhara,
and Mūla-bandhas, the wind, entering the Suṣumṇā through its upward orientation, abandons its coming and going.

The fortunate one here drinks the stream of nectar falling from the moon, which has been heated by the contractions of the downward-moving breath (apāna)—contractions that serve as kindled flames for the fire maintained within the body. 7.

I worship that Knowledge in the form of pure *kumbhaka* (retention), which arises from the ripening of the practice of the three *bandhas*, is devoid of *recaka* (exhalation) and *pūraka* (inhalation), and dries up the flow toward sense objects. 8.

In the unstruck (anāhata) consciousness, experienced by those who are vigilant and heroic in their practice, that glory of the absolute breath-retention (kevala-kumbhaka) unfolds, wherein the movement of both breath and mind has been brought to a standstill. 9.
In the haṭha practices, let the jars (kumbhas) be accompanied by inhalation and exhalation;
however, in the supreme jar (kumbhottama), only the pure jar is envisioned, wherein there is neither the natural nor the modified [breathing] of the vital breath known as recaka and pūraka.
When the inner organ named Trikūṭa is stilled and the ether is fixed by means of the pure kumbhaka breath-retention,
the vital breath immediately attains dissolution, leaving behind the channels of the sun and the moon.
Drawn back by means of the solitary kumbhaka, the vital breath— remaining as the residue after being consumed by the awakened kuṇḍalī—
slowly dissolves within the space of Viṣṇu’s foot (the crown of the head) via the path leading inward.

Through the restraint of unrestrained exhalations by means of what are known as the exclusive *kumbhaka* breath-retentions, there arises for the great-minded a certain dissolution of the vital air (*marut*) that is devoid of the functioning of all the senses. (13)
When Rājayoga is fully developed, there is neither the observation of signs nor the binding of the mind, neither concern for place or time, nor the obstruction of breath,
nor even the exertion of concentration and meditation.
For those established here in Rājayoga, who have abandoned the vision consisting of all visible objects,
there is neither waking nor the state of deep sleep, neither life nor death— how wondrous!

For those whose minds are firmly established in the Śrī Rājayoga, having abandoned everything consisting of "I" and "mine," there is neither the state of a seer nor the existence of an object seen; that which unfolds is pure consciousness alone. 16.

May that Manonmanī abide within me— she by whom the eyes are rendered free from opening and closing, the breath is devoid of exhalation and inhalation, and the mind is empty of both volition and doubt.
When the movement of the breath has been stilled through the long restraint of the mind and the senses, those masters of self-restraint,
with limbs as motionless as lamps in a windless place, become absorbed in the state of *manonmanī*.
O wise one, we shall point out to you a single means for attaining the state of *unmanī*:
while observing the phenomenal world with indifference, uproot your mental constructs with vigilance. (19)
The mind, remaining constantly vigilant in shattering the succession of volitions, gradually attains peace as it diminishes through the disappearance of its objective supports. (20)
We behold the manifestation of the "mindless" (amanaska) mudrā among the foremost of sages, through their restrained cessation of breath, their motionless bodies, and their lotus-eyes half-closed.

These yogis, together with Indra, as the innate notions of "I" and "mine" become slackened due to the absence of the mind, attain a state that transcends the mind, devoid of the movement of the vital airs, and remaining as pure as the sky. || 22 ||

When, having abandoned all other states of being, shall I—having withdrawn all my senses and engaged in the yoga of the Supreme Self—attain that innate, thought-free state which consists of pure consciousness? 23.

When men’s attachment to ancient perfumes has fled due to the excellence of inward self-reflection, there may arise a certain sleep free from dullness, which completely abandons thought of the phenomenal world. 24.
When the roots of conceptualization and mental construction have been severed and the entire web of karma has been utterly uprooted,
that most auspicious yoga-sleep unfolds within the yogin through the power of uninterrupted practice.

O friend, having attained rest upon the couch of the Fourth state, which stands above the triad of states beginning with the Viśva, enjoy at all times that indescribable, thought-free sleep consisting of pure consciousness. 26.
When the sun of the Supreme Self shines forth and the entire darkness of ignorance perishes, alas, O wise ones, even those with stainless vision do not perceive this entire world at all! 27.

When shall I ever attain such a perfection in meditative absorption, wherein the mind has dissolved, within the hollows of the peaks of Śrīśaila—when creepers entwine my body and birds build their nests upon my ears? (28)
Let this intellect wander in non-conceptual samādhi or upon the pair of jar-like breasts of those with antelope-like eyes;
let it move among the dull-witted or within the thoughts of the virtuous—yet the merits and defects fashioned by the intellect do not touch me, the All-pervading Lord.

Thus ends the Yogatārāvalī, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya).
